newsitem.title: UK: Dlr ends firmer in Europe amid erratic cross moves.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends firmer in Europe amid erratic cross moves.

text.p: The dollar ended firmer against the mark and yen in Europe compared with Friday's close but dealers preferred to maintain existing ranges ahead of an event-packed week and as the mark's European cross rates traded erratically.

The dollar got a boost against the yen after comments from Japanese prime minister Ryutaro Hashimoto suggested action from Group of Seven industrialised nations (G7) to weaken the dollar was unlikely. G7 finance ministers meet Saturday in Berlin.
Analysts said the dollar was also underpinned by residual expectations the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy-making Open Market Committee (FOMC) may raise interest rates this week.
The FOMC holds a two-day meeting tomorrow and Wednesday.
Other major events of the week include the Bundesbank weekly council meeting on Thursday, the UK monthly monetary meeting on Wednesday and the U.S. January employment report on Friday.

"The dollar was not the primary mover today but it's been buoyed by the outside chance of an FOMC move and its distance from growing jitters in peripheral European markets," said Klaus Baader, currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
At 1644 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.2430/35 compared with 1.6363/67 late Friday., Against the yen, it was at 121.76/86 compared with 121.10/15 late last week.
Key U.S. economic data out today, meantime, put little additional pressure on the Fed to boost rates this week.

The National Association of Purchasing Management's index of business activity fell to 52.0 in January from a revised 53.8 the previous month, even though its employment and prices indices edged higher.
No action from the FOMC, however, will likely see attention switch immediately to the January employment report and the weekend G7 meeting for fresh direction.
"The G7 is going to provide more a positive than a negative pulse for the dollar," said Joe Prendergast at Merrill Lynch.

"The G7 may have a bit of problem with the speed of the dollar move this year but there will be few who will argue with the direction or the levels and this will be made clear," said Prendergast, who is a foreign exchange strategist at Merrill.
Hashimoto's comments earlier stressed Japan's discomfort with excessive currency moves but he saw no G7 discussion of a dollar reversal.
"Is it possible to lower the value of the dollar through international cooperation? I don't think that's the feeling at the moment," Hashimoto said.
In Europe, monetary union was again centre stage.
The Spanish peseta skidded lower, forcing Bank of Spain intervention to prop it up near its central rate in the European exchange rate mechanism at 85.07 per mark.
The lira remained subdued, however, despite some interim relief that Eurostat's review of budgetary accounting measures ahead of EMU did rule against any key Italian measures yet.

The cloud over the lira and peseta is a rise in concern about Germany's willingness to accept their membership of the first wave of EMU. German government adviser Horst Siebert told an Italian newspaper today that Germany is concerned Italy would "import" instability to the euro.
"There was diverse price action today which can best be explained by bond flows out," said DMG's Baader. "Germany's stance against a broad start to EMU is hardening."
"Basically investors in Italian and Spanish bonds have had a wonderful run, but as volatility rises again they are simply not getting paid enough for the increased risks," said Baader.

Sterling bounced back from Friday's slide, meantime, and staged a rally. A rise in the January UK Purchasing Managers index suggested the pound's rise may not yet be a major problem for UK exporters, analysts said.
--Mike Dolan, London newsroom +44 171 542 6762
